definition: Oja's learning rule, or simply Oja's rule, named after Finnish computer scientist Erkki Oja (Finnish pronunciation: [ˈojɑ], AW-yuh), is a model of how neurons in the brain or in artificial neural networks change connection strength, or learn, over time.
details: It is a modification of the standard Hebb's Rule that, through multiplicative normalization, solves all stability problems and generates an algorithm for principal components analysis. This is a computational form of an effect which is believed to happen in biological neurons.

explainer.lead: Oja's rule is a model of how neurons, biological or artificial, change connection strength over time. It matters because it modifies Hebb's rule with multiplicative normalization, removing stability problems and yielding a principal components analysis algorithm.

tiers.eli5: Like strengthening a path each time it is used, but automatically scaling all paths down so the network doesn't blow up.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it as a stable, normalized Hebbian update that extracts principal components. A pitfall is treating it as a general-purpose learning rule rather than a PCA-oriented one.
tiers.paperLevel: It is a modification of standard Hebb's rule in which multiplicative normalization solves all stability problems and generates an algorithm for principal components analysis; it is believed to be a computational form of an effect in biological neurons.

explainer.example: A network trained with Oja's rule converges to the principal components of its input rather than growing unstable as plain Hebbian learning would.
